title: Why Is There a Barcode on Everything?
parts: The first product ever scanned with today's barcode at a supermarket checkout was a pack of chewing gum.
Later, some people even claimed the stripes hid the mark of the beast.
Pick up a can of soup, a phone charger, a pack of gum. They all carry the same patch of black stripes.
How did it end up on everything?
The story starts with a complaint, and a doodle in the sand.
At the checkout, a person reads every price and punches it in.
According to the story, one grocery boss wished the checkout could read a product by itself.
Bernard Silver, a graduate student at Drexel in Philadelphia, heard about it. He and Norman Joseph Woodland started looking for an answer.
Their first try used a special ink, but it faded too easily and cost too much.
Then Woodland went to Miami Beach to think. Inspired by Morse code, he drew long and short lines in the sand with his fingers.
Then he swept the lines around into a circle, like a target, so a machine could read it from any angle.
They filed a patent in 1949, and it was granted in 1952.
But the world was not ready. The machines to read it quickly, and affordable computers to make sense of it, did not exist yet.
Later, shops wanted it. Checkouts took a lot of staff time, and grocers made very little profit on each sale.
But every chain used its own numbers, and a code only works if everybody shares one.
So in 1970, the grocery industry formed a committee to pick one.
Makers did not want to redo packages while few shops had scanners, and shops doubted scanners would pay off.
Several companies pitched designs, including a round target from RCA.
The winner was a rectangle.
An IBM engineer named George Laurer designed it from scratch.
Straight bars printed better than the round target.
The committee chose it in March 1973, and it became the Universal Product Code.
On June 26, 1974, at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio, Clyde Dawson went to the checkout.
Cashier Sharon Buchanan scanned his item: a pack of Juicy Fruit gum.
Legend says he chose it on purpose, because nobody was sure stripes could be printed on something that small.
It was the first product ever scanned with the new code at a store checkout.
But not everybody cheered.
Unions feared losing jobs.
Consumer groups worried about wrong prices, and about shops keeping track of what people buy.
In 1976, several states required price stickers to stay on the items, which slowed things down.
There was also a strange rumour. Some people claimed the long guard lines hid the number six, six, six.
Laurer called it a coincidence. His first, middle and last names have six letters each.
In the 1980s, big stores like Kmart and Walmart began demanding barcodes on clothing, and the stripes spread everywhere.
Makers could see what was selling, straight from the checkout.
Even the numbers under the bars have a job: a backup, in case the scanner cannot read the stripes.
So that patch of stripes on your soup can is a doodle in the sand, a committee, and a pack of chewing gum.
And speaking of prices, why does a bucket of popcorn at the cinema cost so much?
